source_refs.note: Topic 19.8 with Quick Check 19.6, answered (PDF 50-51); the mechanisms are redrawn. The propagation steps of methane chlorination are given for the stages the book names. The HBr addition is shown with its carbocation step. Answers need review.

blocks.text: A mechanism is the pathway a reaction follows, showing the bonds that break and form as the substrate turns into the product. Mechanisms are of two main types, depending on the reagent: free-radical and ionic (polar). Curly arrows show the movement of a pair of electrons, from where the electrons are to where they go.

This involves homolysis, producing free radicals that attack the substrate. An example is the chlorination of methane in diffused sunlight, which overall can go as far as CH4 + 4Cl2 -> CCl4 + 4HCl. The reaction has three stages: initiation, in which light splits Cl2 into two Cl. radicals; propagation, in which radicals react to form products and more radicals (Cl. + CH4 -> HCl + .CH3, then .CH3 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + Cl.); and termination, in which two radicals combine and the chain stops.

items: Nucleophilic substitution: a nucleophile attacks a saturated, electrophilic carbon and replaces another group, the leaving group, e.g. OH- + CH3Br -> CH3OH + Br- through a transition state.

Nucleophilic addition: a nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbon of a carbonyl compound, giving an addition product, e.g. CN- adds to ethanal and the anion takes H+ from HCN, giving 2-hydroxypropanenitrile.
Electrophilic addition: an electrophile attacks an electron-rich site such as a C=C or C triple bond, e.g. HBr adds to ethene giving bromoethane.
Elimination: two atoms or groups are removed from neighbouring carbon atoms, forming a double or triple bond, e.g. OH- removes H from bromoethane as Br- leaves, giving ethene.

blocks.alt: Two mechanisms. Top: HO- with a lone pair; a curly arrow from it to the delta+ carbon of CH3Br and another from the C-Br bond to Br; a bracketed transition state HO...C...Br with a negative charge; products CH3OH and Br-. Bottom: CN- with a lone pair on C attacks the delta+ carbonyl carbon of ethanal while the C=O pi electrons move onto O, giving CH3-CH(O-)-CN; with HCN this gives CH3-CH(OH)-CN and CN-.
blocks.caption: Nucleophilic substitution and nucleophilic addition (original mechanisms after the book's diagrams).
blocks.long_description: In nucleophilic substitution the hydroxide ion uses its lone pair to bond to the slightly positive carbon while the C-Br bond breaks and bromide leaves; for an instant both are partly bonded in the transition state. In nucleophilic addition the cyanide ion bonds to the carbonyl carbon, the C=O pi electrons move onto oxygen, and the oxygen anion then takes a proton from HCN, regenerating cyanide.

blocks.alt: Two mechanisms. Top: a curly arrow from the C=C of ethene to the delta+ H of H-Br and another from the H-Br bond to Br, giving the carbocation H3C-CH2+ and Br-; Br- then attacks the positive carbon to give CH3-CH2-Br. Bottom: HO- attacks an H on one carbon of bromoethane, the C-H electrons move into the C-C bond and the C-Br electrons go to Br, giving CH2=CH2, H2O and Br-.
blocks.caption: Electrophilic addition and elimination (original mechanisms after the book's diagrams).
blocks.long_description: In electrophilic addition the electron-rich double bond attacks the slightly positive hydrogen of HBr; this gives a carbocation and a bromide ion, which then bond. In elimination the hydroxide ion removes a hydrogen from the carbon next to the C-Br carbon; the C-H electrons form the new pi bond and bromide leaves, giving ethene.

blocks.prompt: Describe NH3, Br. (a bromine atom), H2O, NO2+ and Cl(delta+) as electrophile, nucleophile or free radical.
blocks.explanation: NH3: nucleophile; Br.: free radical; H2O: nucleophile; NO2+: electrophile; Cl(delta+): electrophile.

blocks.prompt: Classify: (i) CH3CH=CH2 + HBr -> CH3CHBrCH3; (ii) CH4 + Br2 -> CH3Br + HBr; (iii) CH3CH2CHClCH3 -> CH3CH2CH=CH2 + HCl.

blocks.explanation: (i) condensation (two molecules join with loss of water); (ii) reduction (gain of hydrogen), which is also an addition.

items: Free-radical: initiation, propagation, termination (e.g. chlorination of methane).
Ionic: nucleophilic substitution, nucleophilic addition, electrophilic addition, elimination.
Curly arrows show electron pairs moving.
